newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Arthuis says all EU members want budget pact deal.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis says all EU members want budget pact deal.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Monday that all EU member states were keen to reach an agreement on a budget stability pact meant to prevent countries from running up big budget deficits after the launch of the single European currency in 1999.

European Union finance ministers postponed a decision on the pact after a day of talks here on Monday, but agreed to reconvene for further discussions on December 12 on the eve of a summit of EU heads of state in Dublin.
"We are near to an agreement. The will to conclude (an agreement) is shared by all members states," Arthuis told a news conference after the meeting.
"All member states want to agree this stability pact."

The talks foundered on the question of how to define the exceptional circumstances -- such as a severe recession -- which would exempt a member state from being fined if it ran up a deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product. Arthuis reiterated France's position that if a country had undergone a recession of more than two percent, it would be exempt from fines.
"Below this level, the council (of ministers) needs to retain all the margin for judgement," he said. "We must not lock ourselves into any automaticity."

Germany had argued that countries be automatically subject to sanctions unless they had suffered a recession over two percent. Arthuis said he believed a majority of member states shared France's view.

A senior European source said there was no question that the discussions over the stability pact had pitted France against Germany. He said some other countries had taken a harder line against Bonn in the discussions.
The dispute over the stability pact has created some tension between Paris and Bonn, fuelling an impression among economists of a potential policy rift between Europe's two leading economies.

It has also coincided with calls by some French politicians for a review of France's decade-old policy of linking the franc to the mark and possible depreciation of the franc. The government has said it does not believe there is any need to change the franc-mark parity.

The senior European source said he did not believe there was any good reason to link the franc-mark exchange rate to the stability pact and said the question of currency parities or exchange rate policy was not discussed during the talks in Brussels.

Some economists see the stability pact as a way of ensuring the strength of the new euro at its launch in 1999 and fear this will run counter to a French wish to use monetary union as a means to get the dollar revalued against European currencies.
